description: The peace of mind that comes from understanding a changing Earth.
summary: Asaase ("earth" in Twi) is a free web app that uses NASA–ISRO's new NISAR L-band radar to show how Ghana's land and water change during the rainy season, when cloud hides them from optical satellites. It tells two stories. Along the Offin River, NISAR maps about 150 km² of illegal gold-mining (galamsey) scars, and Sentinel-1 shows they have grown about 2.5 times since 2021, with about 960 ha inside forest reserves. On the White Volta, NISAR watched the 2026 flood after Burkina Faso's Bagré Dam spill rise and fall in eight weeks, peaking at 12 km² on 21 September near about 3,400 people. Anyone can scrub through every radar pass, click a spot for its history in plain language, and share a view as an image. Every result is checked against independent data. This matters because the people who protect forests and respond to floods in Ghana need to see change when it happens, not after the clouds clear.
details:
What it does: Asaase turns NISAR radar into a map anyone can read on a phone:

  • Where the forest went (galamsey): mining scars along the Offin River on every NISAR pass from June to October 2026, a ten-year view from Sentinel-1 (2016–2026), five forest reserves with how much of each is scarred, and Perseus Mining's licensed Edikan mine outlined and kept apart from galamsey.
  • The Volta breathes (floods): new open water and flooded vegetation on every pass on the White Volta (Pwalugu to Daboya), the people living within 1 km of the water, and the nearest settlements.
  • How radar sees: a plain-language explainer of why radar sees through cloud, and why stripped forest goes dark and flooded vegetation goes bright.
  • Click any spot for its radar history; compare two passes side by side; listen to the story read aloud; share the view as an image for WhatsApp. Light and dark themes; it works on mobile data.

How it works: A Python pipeline (h5py, rasterio, NumPy) downloads NISAR L2 GCOV (HH and HV backscatter) and GUNW (coherence) products from NASA's ASF DAAC through Earthdata: 10 passes per area, about 80 GB. It mosaics the frames, removes speckle (Lee filter), aligns every pass to the first by phase correlation, and detects change:

  • Mining scars: stripping the canopy collapses the HV echo, from about −11 dB in forest to −17 dB in the scars. Scars are HV below −15 dB, a threshold set by overlaying the radar on satellite imagery in five areas.
  • Floods: each pass is compared with a dry-season baseline. New open water darkens by 3 dB or more. Flooded vegetation brightens in HH by 3 dB or more, and by 1.5 dB more than HV, because the pulse bounces off the water and then the stems.

The pipeline writes about 11 MB of map layers and numbers. The app (React, MapLibre) is a static site on Cloudflare Pages, so there is no server to fail.

How we know it is right.

  • Global Forest Watch (Landsat): 75% of our scars were forest in 2000, and its forest-loss record rises, dips and surges in the same years as our radar series.
  • A second radar, Sentinel-1: where NISAR saw flooding, 26% of places brightened by 3 dB or more in mid-September, against 1.8% of the land around them.
  • Robustness: the flood rules were tested nine ways, and the peak lands on 21 September every time.
  • Data quality: one NISAR pass came 80 m out of place. It was detected, realigned, flagged and left out of the charts.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve: Ghana's Forestry Commission says galamsey has destroyed nearly 9,000 ha of forest reserves, over 5,200 ha of it since 2021. Radar that sees through cloud every 12 days can show new scars and rising water while there is still time to act. Next, we want to cover the whole mining belt (an area is just a bounding box and a NISAR track; the same commands build it), send alerts every 12 days to the Forestry Commission and NADMO, and add Twi, Ewe and Dagbani with native speakers.

Limits we state openly: One NISAR season (June–October 2026) and two study areas. Radar can't tell spill water from rain, or say who is mining. Sentinel-1 is coarser than NISAR, so single years carry noise. Reserve boundaries come from OpenStreetMap, not the official gazette.

Tools: Python 3 (earthaccess, asf_search, h5py, rasterio, pyproj, NumPy, SciPy, pytest); TypeScript, React 18, Vite, MapLibre GL; Cloudflare Pages; Playwright and Lighthouse for testing (accessibility 100).

Opensource, MIT licence.
